newsitem.title: UK: UK stocks to struggle as rate rise prompts jitters.
newsitem.headline: UK stocks to struggle as rate rise prompts jitters.

text.p: London stocks look set to struggle again next week as Wednesday's surprise rate rise and nervousness about Wall Street's recent performance continues to unsettle shares, strategists said on Friday.
While the latest jobs data reinforced evidence of moderate growth in the U.S. economy and may soothe nerves somewhat, worries about domestic inflationary pressures remain.
Investors look likely to grasp the excuse of the U.S. election on November 5 and the Federal Reserve Open Market Committee meeting the week after to stay on the sidelines.
"Unless Wall Street really takes off I don't see anything changing. The election, the FOMC, the UK budget all provide excellent opportunities to do nothing," said one London trader.

October U.S. employment and purchasing managers data should calm worries about rising U.S. rates ahead of the FOMC on November 13 but on Friday proved unable to lift UK shares after a disappointing week which saw the FTSE slip back below 4,000 to its lowest level for a month.
A scarcity of significant economic data is likely to add to the subdued mood as markets mark time ahead of the election in the U.S.
That, however, is not expected to throw up any surprises with Bill Clinton heavily favoured to be re-elected.

"London is wanting to march to the beat of its own drum. America has got events to occupy it for the next week and London is tired. Futures have led the recent pull-back and there's almost a buyers strike," said another trader.

But while the unexpected rise in UK interest rates may have done little to dispel the stock market's equivocal mood it may at least serve to reassure investors that the government remains committed to keeping inflation under control.

Interest rates remain the central concern on both sides of the Atlantic and though UK shares slipped back below the 3,950 level as worries about Wall Street's ability to hold record levels were compounded by the tightening in UK monetary policy, persistent selling pressure failed to materialise.
"There are some nerves about the U.S. but basically we're seeing a clssic consolidation. It's perhaps a bit overdue after the charge up through 4,000," said SBC Warburg strategist George Hodgson.
"Ahead of the U.S. election we're seeing a bit of end-of- week horn pulling-in and not much more than that."
Last week, just day's after the FTSE 100 set a new all-time high of 4,073.2, dealers began to talk of a mood swing in London as Wall Street turned in a series of jittery performances.

After the run-up in share prices from the middle of July some profit-taking was inevitable, say dealers, but there is no evidence that a setback will prove severe, especially with the support provided by still-high institutional cash holdings.

"There's not much evidence of serious selling and the weakness has been largely futures-related. The market's suffering from a bit of a hangover after the interest rate rise," said Credit Lyonnais Laing strategist Corey Miller.
"The election will be the main influence on the U.S. but given the recent numbers out of the U.S., monetary policy's likely to stay on hold at the FOMC."
Technical analysts also remain cautious about the immediate prospects for the market.
"While this is still very much a bull market in the medium term, it will come down short-term," said Credit Suisse analyst David Sneddon.
Friday's break below 3,950 would pave the way to 3,927 and then to major support around 3,910 and 3,900, said Sneddon.
